title: 3x3 Matrices, Determinants, Inverses & Transformations
subject: Further Pure Mathematics
description: Master 3x3 matrix multiplication, determinants, singular matrix conditions, inverse matrix calculation using minors, cofactors, and adjugate, as well as 2D/3D geometric transformations and systems of linear planes.

coreConcepts.name: Singular vs Non-Singular Matrices
coreConcepts.explanation: A matrix is singular if its determinant equals zero. Geometrically, this means the transformation collapses 3D space into a plane, line, or point.

coreConcepts.name: Inverse of a 3x3 Matrix
coreConcepts.explanation: Calculated by finding the matrix of minors, applying alternating signs for cofactors $C$, transposing to find the adjugate matrix, and scaling by $\frac{1}{\det(M)}$.

coreConcepts.name: Systems of Linear Equations (Sheaf of Planes)
coreConcepts.latex: \det(A) = 0 \text{ with consistent equations } \implies \text{infinite solutions (line of intersection / sheaf)}
coreConcepts.explanation: When the determinant of coefficients is zero, planes either have no common points (inconsistent, triangular prism) or intersect along a single line (sheaf of planes).

coreConcepts.name: Mathematical Induction for Matrices
coreConcepts.latex: M^n = \dots \implies \text{Prove } n=1, \text{ assume } n=k, \text{ prove } n=k+1 \text{ via } M^{k+1} = M^k M
coreConcepts.explanation: Standard 4-step proof by induction demonstrating validity for all positive integers $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$.

examinerTraps: Forgetting to transpose the matrix of cofactors when computing the adjugate matrix.
Sign errors when computing cofactors: the alternating sign checkerboard $[+ - +; - + -; + - +]$ is the #1 lost mark in CP1.
Confusing 'consistent equations' with having a unique solution. A system can be consistent with infinitely many solutions if planes form a sheaf.

title: Complex Numbers: Argand Loci, Cubic Roots & De Moivre's Proofs
subject: Further Pure Mathematics
description: Comprehensive guide to complex numbers in A-Level Further Maths: Euler's formula, modulus-argument arithmetic, loci in the Argand plane (circles, half-lines, angle boundaries), and complex conjugate root theorems for polynomials.

coreConcepts.name: Purely Imaginary Proof
coreConcepts.explanation: A complex number is strictly imaginary if and only if its real component vanishes, or $w$ equals the negative of its complex conjugate.

coreConcepts.name: Argand Loci: Circles and Half-Lines
coreConcepts.latex: |z - z_0| = r \text{ (Circle)}, \quad \arg(z - z_0) = \theta \text{ (Half-line radiating from } z_0)
coreConcepts.explanation: Remember that the initial point $z_0$ is open/excluded in half-line loci, and angle bounds represent sectors in the complex plane.

coreConcepts.name: Conjugate Root Theorem
coreConcepts.latex: P(z) = 0 \text{ with real coefficients } \implies \text{roots appear in conjugate pairs } (\alpha \pm i\beta)
coreConcepts.explanation: If a polynomial with real coefficients has $a + bi$ as a root, $a - bi$ must also be a root, allowing quadratic factors $(z - \alpha)^2 + \beta^2$ to be factored out.

examinerTraps: Drawing full lines instead of half-lines/rays for $\arg(z - z_0) = \theta$. The endpoint $z_0$ must be an open circle.
Argument convention errors: $\arg(z)$ must always lie within the principal range $(-\pi, \pi]$.
Failing to multiply by complex conjugates when rationalizing denominators.

title: First & Second Order Differential Equations & Physical Modelling
subject: Further Pure Mathematics
description: Master analytical methods for solving 1st order differential equations using integrating factors, and 2nd order linear non-homogeneous differential equations using auxiliary equations, complementary functions, and particular integrals.

coreConcepts.name: Integrating Factor Method (1st Order)
coreConcepts.explanation: Multiply through by $I(x)$ to express the LHS as $\frac{d}{dx}[y I(x)]$, followed by direct integration.

coreConcepts.name: Second Order Auxiliary Equation
coreConcepts.latex: a\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + b\frac{dy}{dx} + cy = f(x) \implies am^2 + bm + c = 0
coreConcepts.explanation: Roots determine Complementary Function ($y_{CF}$): distinct real roots ($Ae^{m_1 x} + Be^{m_2 x}$), repeated roots ($(A + Bx)e^{mx}$), or complex roots ($e^{px}[A\cos(qx) + B\sin(qx)]$). General Solution is $y = y_{CF} + y_{PI}$.

coreConcepts.name: Particular Integral Trials
coreConcepts.latex: f(x) = k e^{\lambda x} \implies y_{PI} = C e^{\lambda x} \quad (\text{or } C x e^{\lambda x} \text{ if } \lambda \text{ is a root of auxiliary})
coreConcepts.explanation: Carefully choose trial functions that avoid duplicating terms in the complementary function.

examinerTraps: Applying initial boundary conditions to the Complementary Function before finding the Particular Integral.
Algebraic slip in differentiating particular integrals with product rule.
Forgetting absolute values in $\int \frac{1}{x} dx = \ln|x|$ which affects sign in real-world modelling constraints.

title: Hyperbolic Functions, Maclaurin Series & Inverse Trigonometry
subject: Further Pure Mathematics
description: Comprehensive breakdown of hyperbolic functions $(\sinh, \cosh, \tanh)$, logarithmic forms of inverse hyperbolics, Maclaurin and Taylor expansions, and derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions.

coreConcepts.name: Definitions & Identities
coreConcepts.latex: \cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}, \quad \sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}, \quad \cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1
coreConcepts.explanation: Osborn's Rule states that standard trig identities convert to hyperbolic identities with the sign reversed when two sines multiply (e.g. $\sin^2 \to -\sinh^2$).

coreConcepts.name: Inverse Trigonometric & Hyperbolic Derivatives
coreConcepts.explanation: Derived using implicit differentiation and standard Pythagorean identities.

coreConcepts.name: Maclaurin Series Expansion
coreConcepts.explanation: Expansion of smooth functions around $x=0$. Often combined with Leibniz's theorem for $n$-th derivatives.

examinerTraps: Confusing trig identities with hyperbolic identities: forgetting the sign flip in $\cosh(2x) = \cosh^2 x + \sinh^2 x$.
Not stating the range of validity for Maclaurin series.
Missing the $\pm$ distinction in $\text{arcosh } x = \ln(x + \sqrt{x^2-1})$ for $x \ge 1$.

title: Polar Coordinates: Curves, Tangents & Area Integration
subject: Further Pure Mathematics
description: Understand polar curve sketching ($r = f(\theta)$ like cardioids, limaçons, and lemniscates), vertical and horizontal tangents via Cartesian conversion $(x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta)$, and polar bounded area calculation.

coreConcepts.name: Cartesian Conversion & Tangents
coreConcepts.latex: x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta \implies \frac{dx}{d\theta} = 0 \text{ (Vertical Tangent)}, \quad \frac{dy}{d\theta} = 0 \text{ (Horizontal Tangent)}
coreConcepts.explanation: Tangents parallel to the initial line have $\frac{dy}{d\theta} = 0$, while tangents perpendicular to the initial line have $\frac{dx}{d\theta} = 0$.

coreConcepts.name: Polar Area Integration
coreConcepts.explanation: Always identify symmetry lines to simplify integration limits, and check for negative $r$ bounds.

examinerTraps: Forgetting the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in the polar area formula $\frac{1}{2} \int r^2 d\theta$.
Incorrect limits of integration when curves pass through the pole ($r=0$).
Failing to differentiate using the product rule on $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$.

title: Summation of Series, Method of Differences & Vectors in 3D
subject: Further Pure Mathematics
description: Techniques for evaluating finite series using standard summation formulas $\sum r, \sum r^2, \sum r^3$ and method of differences (telescoping series), alongside 3D vectors (skew lines, planes, dot & cross products) and polynomial root relations.

coreConcepts.name: Method of Differences
coreConcepts.explanation: Terms cancel telescopically leaving only the boundary terms from the beginning and end.

coreConcepts.name: Vieta's Formulas for Polynomial Roots
coreConcepts.explanation: Relations between the coefficients of a polynomial equation and sums/products of its roots.

coreConcepts.name: 3D Vectors: Planes & Lines
coreConcepts.explanation: Scalar product form of a plane $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=d$ reveals the normal vector immediately for distance and angle calculations.

examinerTraps: Leaving uncancelled terms in telescopic series, especially when fractions have shifts like $f(r) - f(r+2)$.
Vector distance formula: misidentifying normal vector magnitude.
